title: India Demonstrates First Free-Space Quantum Link Over 5.56 km of Air
excerpt: QNu Labs' overnight trial between BISAG-N and IIT Gandhinagar transmitted secure encryption keys through open air with an error rate below 5%, laying the groundwork for satellite-based quantum communication.
body:
• India demonstrated its first free-space Quantum Key Distribution link over 5.56 km in a field trial conducted on the night of Sept. 27-28 by QNu Labs with BISAG-N and IIT Gandhinagar, the Ministry of Electronics and IT announced on Oct. 3.
  • The trial transmitted encryption keys through open air — no fibre — using QNu Labs' Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking system, achieving a stable Quantum Bit Error Rate below 5% and generating secure keys at 230-260 bits per second.
  • The keys were integrated with BISAG-N's post-quantum cryptography platform, Vedic Kavach, enabling successful end-to-end encryption and decryption of test messages.
  • Free-space QKD is the missing link between fibre-based quantum networks and satellite quantum links — the only way to secure communications that pass through space — and the demonstration paves the way for longer-distance and satellite-based quantum-secure networks.

India has demonstrated its first free-space Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) link, establishing a secure quantum communication channel across 5.56 kilometres of open air between the Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N) and IIT Gandhinagar, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology announced on Saturday.

The field trial was conducted on the night of Sept. 27-28 by QNu Labs, an Indian quantum-secure digital infrastructure company, in collaboration with BISAG-N and IIT Gandhinagar. Using the company's Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking system to hold the free-space optical link steady, the system maintained a stable Quantum Bit Error Rate below 5 per cent while generating secure encryption keys at a rate of 230-260 bits per second.

The keys were then integrated with BISAG-N's post-quantum cryptography platform, Vedic Kavach, enabling successful end-to-end encryption and decryption of test messages — a complete loop from quantum key generation to applied cryptography.

Context & Background

Quantum Key Distribution uses the laws of quantum physics to generate and share encryption keys: any attempt to intercept the key disturbs the quantum states being transmitted, revealing the eavesdropper. Free-space transmission — sending the keys as light pulses through open air rather than through fibre-optic cable — is the essential technology for long-distance and satellite links, where fibre simply cannot run.

https://x.com/DDNewslive/status/2106698430852763840

The demonstration is significant precisely because it breaks the fibre constraint, making it directly relevant to future satellite-based quantum communication systems. A laser link that works through 5.56 km of night air is the terrestrial proving ground for links to orbiting satellites, where the channel passes through the full atmosphere.

The trial combined two complementary layers of quantum security. On the hardware side, QNu Labs deployed its Armos QKD device over the free-space optical channel to generate and distribute the quantum keys. On the software side, BISAG-N's Vedic Kavach provided software-based post-quantum cryptography and quantum random number generation. The integrated architecture is designed to remain resilient even when the physical quantum communication channel is temporarily unavailable.

Impact & Analysis

For India's strategic communications, the trial is a concrete step toward encryption that survives the quantum era. Today's widely used public-key cryptography is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful future quantum computers; governments and financial institutions are racing to deploy quantum-resistant alternatives. A working free-space QKD link gives India an indigenous path to securing defence, diplomatic and financial communications rather than depending on foreign technology.

The commercial signal matters too. QNu Labs, an Indian deep-tech company, designed the QKD device, the tracking system and the field trial — evidence that the country's quantum stack is moving from laboratory research to fielded, integrated systems.

"The successful 5.56-km demonstration paved the way for longer-distance quantum-secure networks and satellite-based quantum communication."

— Sunil Gupta, Co-founder and CEO, QNu Labs

Dr. Vinay Thakur, Director General of BISAG-N, said the integration of Vedic Kavach with QNu Labs' QKD technology marked "a significant step towards practical quantum-resilient communication systems." Cmde Manish Tripathi (Retd), in-charge of the ISTF at IIT Gandhinagar, added that the demonstration provided a valuable field environment for advancing practical quantum communication technologies — and a showcase of how academia, indigenous technology and real-world experimentation can be combined.

Diaspora Angle

The trial will matter first to banks, governments and defence agencies — not to everyday users. But the trajectory is worth watching: every online transaction, from a UPI payment to an NRI remittance, depends on encryption standards that the quantum era will force the world to replace. India's move to build that replacement layer domestically means the diaspora's financial and communication links to India will ultimately rest on systems tested and owned at home.

What's Next

The stated next step is distance: the path forward runs through longer free-space spans and, eventually, satellite-based QKD — the only architecture that can carry quantum keys across continents. Watch for longer-range trials, integration with live networks rather than test messages, and the country's quantum roadmap turning field trials into operational infrastructure.
